phonemes.desc: Bilabial nasal [m], the first consonant of the word mꜣꜥt
Glottal stop [ʔ], Egyptological alef; some scholars vocalise this as a light 'a' glide
Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ], the ayin that gives the root its throaty core
Voiceless alveolar stop [t], the feminine ending that turns the verbal root into the abstract noun 'truth'

pronunciation.approximation: 'mah-ʿAHT' — a soft 'm', a deep throaty 'ah' in the middle, and a crisp final 't'.

kin.label: Egyptian
kin.form: mꜣꜥt, the standard hieroglyphic spelling of Maat with the feather of truth (Faulkner, s.v.)

kin.label: Coptic
kin.form: ⲙⲉ (me), also ⲙⲏⲉ (mēe), 'truth, righteousness', the late reflex of mꜣꜥt (Crum, s.v. ⲙⲉ)

kin.label: Root
kin.form: mꜣꜥ, 'straight, right, true' — the verb of straightness that becomes the cosmic principle (Allen 2013)

pronunciation.note: Mꜣꜥt is a Tier-1 restoration of a consonantal Egyptian word. The Egyptological alef (ꜣ) and ayin (ꜥ) are both preserved, marking two different throat sounds that English lacks — distinctive letters the ASCII form loses. The final -t is the feminine abstract ending; the word literally means 'straightness' or 'rightness'.

domains.title: Truth, Justice, Order
domains.subtitle: The domain of Mꜣꜥt
domains.lead: Mꜣꜥt is the Egyptian cosmos made moral: truth, straightness, the even plumb line, the feather against which the heart is weighed. Not a law code but a state of being — the king upholds her, the priest recites her, the scribe writes her, and the justified dead speak her name before the gods. To live in Maat is to move in harmony with the structure of reality itself.

cards.name: Feather of Truth
cards.desc: The heart of the deceased is weighed against Maat's feather; only the light heart passes the tribunal.

cards.name: Cosmic Order
cards.desc: Re 'lives on Maat' each morning; without her, the sun would not rise and chaos would rush back in.

cards.name: Straightness
cards.desc: Maat is the plumb line, the even measure, the straight path that kings, priests, and scribes must keep.

cards.name: Kingly Offering
cards.desc: Pharaohs presented small figures of Maat to the gods, ritually restoring order to its divine source.

mythology.lead: Maat has no cycle of adventures — she is Egypt's most abstract major power, a principle wearing a woman's face. Her 'myths' are therefore texts: the creation theology that makes order prior to the world, the judgement scene that made her feather the most famous image of Egyptian religion, and the wisdom literature that turned her into the common man's cause.

myths.title: Order Before the World
myths.text: Egyptian creation theology insists that order precedes the world rather than following it. On the Shabaka Stone — the Late Period copy of the Memphite Theology — Ptah conceives creation 'through the heart' (thought) and 'through the tongue' (the commanding word), and the text closes its account with the consequence in the vocabulary of Maat: justice is done for the one who does what is loved, and punishment for the one who does what is hated. Sun hymns make the dependence still more intimate. The great hymn of Book of the Dead spell 15B addresses the sun as one who lives upon Maat, and temple tradition calls Maat the daughter of Re — the very air the sun-god breathes, set at his nose. Without her the sun would not rise and the chaos before creation would rush back: Maat is not a rule the cosmos obeys but the medium it breathes. The theology turns morality into physics — and physics, remarkably, into something worth keeping.

myths.title: The Weighing of the Heart
myths.text: The most famous scene in Egyptian religion survives on the Papyrus of Ani (BM EA 10470, c. 1250 BCE) at the head of Book of the Dead spell 125. The scribe Ani's heart — his conscience made organ — is set in the pan of a balance against a single ostrich feather, Maat herself, the minimum possible weight of a life. Anubis crouches at the scales, adjusting the plumb line; Thoth, ibis-headed, waits with palette to record the verdict; behind the god crouches Ammit the Devourer, crocodile-headed, lion-fronted, hippopotamus-backed, for the hearts that fail. Before the tribunal's assessors the deceased recites the Negative Confession — 'I have not committed evil against men... I have not diminished the offerings in the temples... I have not made anyone weep' — forty-two denials for the forty-two judges. A heart exactly level with Maat is declared 'true of voice' and crosses to the Field of Reeds. The scene's genius is its unit of measurement: a feather. Ethics is weighed not in laws broken but in lightness — the only guilt is heaviness.

myths.title: The King Gives Maat Back
myths.text: If Maat flows from the gods to the world, Egyptian ritual sent it back. From the New Kingdom onward, temple walls at Karnak, Luxor, and Abydos show a recurring scene: the king, tiny before the colossal god, lifts a seated statuette of Maat — a woman with a single feather — and presents her to Amun-Re or Osiris. The gesture says that justice is not the monarch's possession but his loan; he returns it to its source so that order can circulate again from god to king to field and river. Hymns make the circuit explicit — the king 'offers Maat to the lord of Maat', and Maat comes to the one she loves. The ritual did not flatter the king; it audited him. Each presentation was a receipt for a reign's conduct, and the tiny statuette in pharaoh's arms is one of antiquity's most lucid images of government as trusteeship: power standing before its source with the evidence in its hands, returning what was only ever lent.

myths.title: The Peasant's Appeal
myths.text: Egypt's most searching meditation on Maat is not a myth but a story: the Tale of the Eloquent Peasant (Papyrus Berlin 3023), a Middle Kingdom masterpiece. A poor farmer, robbed of his goods by a corrupt steward, petitions the high official Rensi nine times, and his speeches are a running treatise — 'Do Maat for the Lord of Maat', he cries, 'for Maat is not carried off; it endures, and him who reaches it, it leads to blessedness.' Each petition grows more eloquent and is ignored with equal artistry, until the exasperated king himself orders the steward to keep listening — the audience, not the verdict, being the tale's point about courts. When justice finally comes, it comes because speech aligned with Maat outlasted indifference. The peasant's refrain became Egyptian literature's most quoted line on law: justice delayed is the system's default, and the only weapon the powerless own is the demand that it not be. Few ancient texts let a beggar lecture the state; Egypt canonized the lecture.

lore.syncretism: Maat resisted translation. The Greeks, who happily equated Amun with Zeus and Hathor with Aphrodite, had no goddess of cosmic correctness to offer, and later writers reach instead for abstractions — Dikē, Justice, or the Stoic notion of a rational order governing gods and men alike; Plutarch's treatise on Isis discusses Maat-like concepts under Greek ethical categories rather than any divine name. Inside Egypt the syncretisms ran the other way: late theology fused Maat with Isis as 'the great god's mother, lady of Maat', and paired her constantly with Thoth — the divine couple of the two intellectual virtues, cosmic order and divine utterance, scholarship married to its standard. In Coptic, Maat survives not as a goddess but as the ordinary word for truth, ⲙⲉ. A deity can be absorbed into the language and disappear from the pantheon in the same gesture — that is Maat's fate, and fittingly, her triumph.
lore.culturalLegacy: Maat's feather is among the most recognized images on earth — the badge of Egyptian judgement, stamped on museum merchandise and book covers, invoked wherever an emblem of conscience is needed. Her name powers a modern ethical revival: Afrocentric and Kemetic movements place Maat at the center of a living moral philosophy, sometimes with an 'ideals of Maat' list derived from the Negative Confession; courts, schools, and community organizations invoke her as the ancient warrant that justice is older than any state. Egyptologists — Assmann's classic study above all — treat her as the key to everything Egyptian: art that renders 'the right way', architecture aligned to cosmic axes, a state whose ideology was a promise of order. And because her name means simply 'right, straight, true', she survives in every language's plea that things be set right. Few abstract nouns have ever carried so much divinity.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Maat is the Egyptian answer to the oldest political question: is justice a human invention or a feature of the universe? Egypt answered without hesitation — a feature of the universe, as real as gravity, which is why the sun depends on it. The answer sounds naive until you notice what it built. A state that measured its legitimacy against an impersonal standard produced four thousand years of obsessive self-audit: kings offering Maat back to the gods, peasants lecturing stewards, scribes copying wisdom books that define the quiet man as the one who has mastered himself.

The standard was flattered more often than obeyed — corrupt stewards are the stock villain of Egyptian literature precisely because the standard existed to be violated. But the flattery matters. A society that must at least pretend its law is cosmic will, over centuries, leave a record that makes the pretense legible. Maat is that pretense hardened into principle: the wager that reality itself is on the side of the straight path, and that a feather is enough to weigh a life against.

lore.archaeology: The material record of Maat is a record of repetition — which is her point. The weighing scene survives in dozens of New Kingdom Book of the Dead papyri, most famously the Papyrus of Ani (BM EA 10470) and of Hunefer (EA 9901,3); temple walls from Karnak to Abydos carry the offering-of-Maat scene from Seti I through Ramesses II; and small votive figures of the kneeling goddess — a woman with a single feather — were dedicated in the thousands, from the gold and lapis amulets of Tutankhamun's treasures to the humble faience examples of Deir el-Medina. The Hall of the Two Maats in the Osireion at Abydos names the standard twice, as if for emphasis. Even scribal palettes and builders' plumb bobs invoke her. An abstract goddess leaves abstract archaeology: not a temple she can call her own, but a civilization aligned, wall by wall, to her axis.
